forecast.desc: As of early August the cumulative seasonal deficit is ~11% below LPA. After the driest June in over a decade (~40% deficit), an above-normal July (+1%, 283.3 mm vs 280.5 mm normal) narrowed it sharply. IMD's outlook is below-normal (<94% LPA) for both August and the Aug–Sep second half as El Niño strengthens; a positive IOD forecast for September is the potential offset. Whole-season print is tracking ~90% of LPA.
forecast.inference: The season proved more resilient than the June collapse implied, but the recovery has stalled into a below-normal August. July's low-pressure systems cut the seasonal deficit from ~40% to ~11%, yet IMD now forecasts below-normal rain (<94% of LPA) for both August and the Aug–Sep second half as El Niño intensifies toward its autumn peak — a firmer below-normal call than the July vintage carried. The distribution has shifted accordingly toward the deficient/below-normal outcome, with the season tracking ~90% of LPA. The one credible upside is the forecast positive IOD in September: it rescued the 1997 monsoon from a comparable El Niño, and it is the variable that could pull the season back.

seasonal.desc: June and July were the most contrasting months of the season. June was the driest in over a decade; July outperformed. The El Niño suppression the spring anticipated for late season is the risk into August–September.
seasonal.inference: The season inverted the textbook Super El Niño script twice: a severe June (contrary to the 'monsoon escapes the peak' thesis), then a strong July recovery as low-pressure systems formed. The back-half risk has now re-emerged — IMD's below-normal call for August and September reflects the strengthening ENSO signal, and August alone carries ~29% of the seasonal total. The genuine swing factor is the Indian Ocean: a positive IOD developing in September would blunt El Niño's suppression the way it did in 1997, turning a below-normal season back toward near-normal.

onset.desc: IMD declared Kerala onset on June 4 — three days later than the June 1 normal, and against pre-season forecasts of an early arrival. Onset stalled at both ends for nearly two weeks.
onset.inference: The late onset was the leading edge of the June collapse — the same weak circulation that delayed arrival produced the ~40% June deficit. Onset stalled at both ends for close to two weeks, and the arrival never became the season's highlight. It is a useful reminder that onset timing is only weakly correlated with the seasonal total: the season went on to recover sharply in July despite the poor start, then faces renewed El Niño pressure into the back half.

reservoir.desc: Live storage across major reservoirs vs the ten-year seasonal normal. The July rains lifted storage off a dire early-July low, but the deficit season leaves it below the normal fill for mid-August.
reservoir.inference: The buffer that kept this a price story rather than a supply-collapse story has recovered but not refilled. Storage climbed from a dire 26% of capacity in early July to ~44% by early August — a big jump — yet that sits below the ten-year normal fill for mid-August, and the southern and eastern basins remain critically low (Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Telangana, Jharkhand, Odisha, West Bengal all well under normal). Aggregate supply is adequate; the live risk stays on price transmission and on the below-normal August–September keeping upward pressure on food inflation into Oct–Dec.

regional.desc: The June–July swing was dramatic and uneven, and the recovery is incomplete. Central India flipped from ~50% deficit to a small seasonal surplus; the northwest rebounded but sits below normal; east/northeast and the south peninsula lagged throughout.

rows.note: Weaker phase through mid-August under below-normal outlook

regional.inference: The regional picture reorganised between June and July but did not fully heal. Central India — the core rain-fed belt and worst-hit in June — swung to a small seasonal surplus, the single biggest positive of the recovery, and the northwest rebounded to ~88% of LPA. The persistent laggards are east/northeast India (~60–70% LPA) and the south peninsula (~77% LPA), which barely improved across both months and now carry the deficit concentration into the El Niño-pressured, below-normal back half. Around 47% of districts were still deficient or large-deficient through July.
